claims.text: The 14 July 2026 consent grants 55,000 options at $0.52 but recites a 6 May 2025 valuation.
The supplied review says the earlier appraisal valued a share at $0.38 and its twelve-month period ended 6 May 2026, 69 days before the grant.
The later appraisal is dated 21 April 2026, concludes $0.52, and was adopted on 18 May 2026; the July consent does not cite it.
The 17 March 2026 consent cites the earlier report's 28 May 2025 issue date rather than its 6 May valuation date.
The supplied review flags a record/valuation mismatch and possible option-holder tax exposure; this design exercise does not independently determine a tax result.
The review requests corrective consents before closing, a purchase-agreement representation covering outstanding grants, and a covenant for the next appraisal refresh.
This is an expressly fictional supplied review. Full appraisals and consents were not supplied; legal conclusions and current law have not been rechecked.

a.html:
1 · What the record says

The 14 July 2026 consent grants 55,000 options at $0.52 per share, but recites a valuation dated 6 May 2025. The supplied review says that earlier appraisal concluded $0.38.

The later appraisal, dated 21 April 2026 and adopted on 18 May, supports the $0.52 figure in the review. It is not named in the July consent. A March consent separately uses the earlier report’s issue date instead of its valuation date.
a.why: A narrative block preserves the finding, supporting detail and requested action.
a.encoding: The heading states the point; the paragraph or aligned table cells retain the material dates, qualifiers and requested action.

a.html:
2 · Why the discrepancy matters

The review distinguishes the option price from the record supporting it. Its stated concern is that the July consent points to the earlier appraisal, 69 days after that appraisal’s twelve-month period ended.

It flags potential tax exposure for the option holder. This sample does not independently establish that a tax charge is due, or that the underlying valuation was unreasonable.
a.why: A narrative block preserves the finding, supporting detail and requested action.
a.encoding: The heading states the point; the paragraph or aligned table cells retain the material dates, qualifiers and requested action.

units.claim: What the review asks for before closing

a.html:
3 · What the review asks for

Correct the July consent to identify the 21 April 2026 appraisal and correct the March recital in the same instrument. Obtain a representation covering outstanding grants and a covenant for the next valuation refresh.

The recommendation is a documented closing follow-up, not a silent edit to the source consent.

sections.heading: What the review identifies
sections.body: The review reports a 55,000-option grant at $0.52 on 14 July 2026. It says the cited May 2025 appraisal valued shares at $0.38, while the later April 2026 appraisal concluded $0.52 and was adopted on 18 May.

sections.heading: What this clip proves—and does not
sections.body: The clip shows the earlier valuation date and itself states $0.52 for that date. The earlier $0.38 figure comes from the supplied review, not this excerpt. The clip does not provide the full grant consent, either appraisal or proof of adoption. Those additional facts come from the supplied review and are not independently verified here.
